title: Preventing migraine: a CGRP antibody
description: CGRP is a signalling molecule released during migraine attacks. Antibodies against it, given as a monthly injection, are a newer way of preventing attacks. One study scanned people with migraine while a painful stimulus was applied to the face, before and two to three weeks after an injection of galcanezumab. Afterwards, the hypothalamus, which is active in the early stages of an attack, responded less, more so in people whose migraines improved. In this episode brightness shows the change since before treatment: violet means less than before.
caveat: All findings come from one study of 26 people with migraine, scanned between attacks during a test with a painful stimulus to the face, not during a migraine attack. A related antibody that blocks the CGRP receptor instead (erenumab) produced a different pattern in an earlier study, so the brain effect depends on the antibody. The source reports no difference from people without migraine, so the first part is drawn at rest. These are averages across groups of people, not a picture of any one person's brain. Treatments help many people, not everyone, and in different ways. This is not medical advice: talk to a doctor or therapist about what is right for you.
